name: Norway
tagline: Free, close to Denmark, and almost entirely in Norwegian
ownCitizens: If you hold Norwegian citizenship, Lånekassen is yours — for everyone else it is realistically closed — and the registration steps for other EU/EEA citizens are not about you. Your IB is still a foreign qualification, so the IB entry rules on this page still apply.
summary: Norway charges EEA students no tuition and sits an hour from Copenhagen. The obstacle is language: Norwegian higher education is taught in Norwegian, several large universities offer no English-taught bachelor programme at all, and the English-taught set nationally is small enough to list. If you take Danish A, that obstacle is lower than it looks: the national admissions service counts Danish A at grade 3 or better as documented Norwegian.
whyConsider: No tuition at public institutions for EEA citizens. Only a semester fee, which is small.
Danish A at grade 3 or better meets the Norwegian language requirement for general admission, so the whole Norwegian-taught system is formally open to an IB student who takes Danish A.

Nordic mobility arrangements are well established, and if you can claim Danish SU, it treats Nordic study more generously than the rest. If you cannot claim it, check your own country's student finance first — several EU/EEA systems fund a full degree in another country.
watchOuts: The documentation window closes on 1 July and IB results are published on 6 July. Samordna opptak's answer: fill in the IB's Request for Results Service with your coordinator, naming the institutions handling your application, and they read your results electronically.
English-taught bachelor programmes are scarce. Check the specific programme rather than the university, because a university with English-taught master’s degrees may have none at bachelor level.
Ranking is binding in an unusual way: an offer on a higher choice makes every lower choice disappear, and you cannot wait-list for one that has gone. The order has to be right by 1 July.
Oslo and Bergen are expensive places to live, and that, rather than tuition, is what a Norwegian year costs.

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: A full IB Diploma gives general admission qualification (generell studiekompetanse). Points convert onto the Norwegian scale, and competitive programmes are decided on that converted number.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: Specific requirements apply to particular programmes, most often mathematics and science at stated Norwegian course levels. Checked per programme rather than nationally.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Scarce. Several of the largest universities offer none at bachelor level, and the national set is small enough to enumerate. Master’s level is a different picture entirely, which is the source of most of the confusion about Norway.
language.englishProof: Set per programme where an English-taught option exists.
notes: Norwegian-taught programmes require documented Norwegian. For an IB applicant, Danish A (higher or standard level) at grade 3 or better documents it; without Danish A you need an approved Norwegian test.

feeContext.summary: No tuition at public institutions. A small compulsory semester fee applies.
Norway introduced tuition for students from outside the EEA and Switzerland. Amounts are set by each institution and are not established here.

sectorLandscape.summary: Norway merged most of its colleges into its universities over the last decade, so the sector looks flatter than the Danish or Dutch one: a smaller number of large, multi-campus universities, alongside specialist institutions and a set of private providers that matter more here than the word "private" suggests elsewhere.

routes.what: Large, often spread across several campuses after the mergers, covering most subjects. Three-year bachelor, two-year master. Teaching is overwhelmingly in Norwegian at bachelor level.
The remaining university colleges, more applied and more regional, strong in nursing, teaching, engineering and business. Fewer than there were, because most merged into universities.

Single-field institutions with university status — the business school BI, the sport sciences school, the music academy, the veterinary and architecture schools. They are easy to miss if you only look at the universities.
routes.note: BI Norwegian Business School is the most likely English-taught bachelor route into Norway, and it is private and charges tuition.

routes.what: Short vocational higher education, half a year to two years, tied closely to a trade or an industry. Applied for through its own route rather than the main portal.
routes.note: Taught in Norwegian. A real tier of Norwegian post-secondary education, but not a realistic route from an IB.

notes: Dates are the published 2026 ones; Samordna opptak had not published the 2027 calendar when this was re-checked on 24 September 2026.

Resolved 24 September 2026: Samordna opptak's IB page says a Diploma candidate completes the IB's Request for Results Service with their coordinator, and the institutions read the grades electronically once they are issued.
The English-taught bachelor programmes are listed institution by institution on the country profile (data/countries/no.json). Tuition charged by private institutions other than BI is not established.
